title: creepr
text:
I really like {beepr}. For the uninitiated, the usage is simply

beepr::beep()

and the result of this code snippet is a beep. Literally a solitary beep. Quite useful when you have a medium length bit of code and want some kind of indication when it has finished. There are a handful of additional noises that can be accessed by placing a number in the function call.
These noises are all fine. But that’s it, they’re just fine. They’re not shocking, jarring, chilling or creepy. Where’s the fun in that?
Turns out, if you do a bit of digging, the {beepr} package provides you with the functionality to play any .wav file that’s on your machine. This can be done with

beepr:::play_file("/path/to/noise.wav")

That got me thinking. If I could collated some creepy .wav files I could probably make a creepy version of {beepr} before Halloween. Probably became a reality and in fact, going from this stupid idea to a working package only took a couple of hours (and I’d forgotten how to make a package).

title: creepr
text:
Get creeping
I’ve put the package on github, thus you can install and run {creepr} in the following way

devtools::install_github("https://github.com/jcken95/creepr")
creepr::creepr()

This will play a sound from my collated sounds at random. I’ve (to date) included a whopping 8 creepy sounds: “creature”, “eerie”, “intense”, “laugh”, “piano”, “piano2”, “ringing” and “strings”.
A feature of this package is that, even if you close R whilst the sound is playing, the sound will not terminate with R. If you play a sound, then you’re committed to it. It’s like tops 15 seconds.
Happy creeping!

title: Code review for statisticians, data scientists & modellers
text:
I work as a data scientist alongside people who typically have academic backgrounds in statistics, epidemiology, or something of a similar feel. Some of us have job titles relating to data science, other to mathematical and statistical modelling. None of us are software developers by trade.
However, we’re writing software all day. We’re writing mathematical/statistical models, creating data-driven products and doing data engineering. We quality assure all of this work via code review.
The honest answer to Who is this for? is that this is for me. It’s for a previous version of myself who knew the mechanics of reviewing code, but could have exercised a bit more much more nuance.
That being said, I think anyone working in some kind of modelling or analytical role, whose main output is some sort of mathematical or statistical analysis, but writes code to implement their models could find this useful.
It doesn’t really matter what programming language you use, or whether you’re storing your code on GitHub, GitLab, BitBucket or whatever else. However this will be biased towards R and GitHub because that’s what I use. The concepts are important here, not the precise toolkit.
If you’re here, I’m going to assume you know roughly what a code review is, but it doesn’t hurt to have a quick refresher.
Code review is a form of peer review. Let’s suppose you’ve written some code, made a pull request (PR) and then assigned a reviewer. The reviewer goes through your code and looks for potential issues with the code, suggests improvements, and maybe says one or two nice things about the thing you’ve been grinding away at.
I’d also like to be upfront here and say there is very little original thought going into this. Software developers have written a lot of good content on what makes good code review. I’ll link to some further reading and inspiration and the end.
My aim here is to:

Bring good code review practice to those in analytical roles.
Communicate this good practice in a way which works for those in analytical roles.

title: Code review for statisticians, data scientists & modellers
text:
Literal code review
Here you’re going to look at the code, maybe run or interact with it, then make comments about the code via the PR mechanisms. I tend to start by having a skim over the code to look for general structure, then spend some time running and interacting with the code later to really get into the guts of it.

Annotating code
To make a comment, click the + symbol to comment on a single line of code. Click a + and drag down to comment on multiple lines.



Making a comment on a line of code.



You can write a general comment or question in the text box.
Click the little +/- symbol (it looks a bit like a page 📄) to make a direction suggestion on the code. This is useful when it’s simply easier to make the fix, than telling someone how to make the fix.
Clicking the symbol again will let you make a new suggestion on the same line(s) of code. Handy when you think there are multiple ways forward.




Making a direct suggestion to code.



Click Add single comment if the review is informal or you’re just being nosey. Start review is better formal reviews.



Submitting review
Once you’ve finished reviewing, click Review changes in the top right of the browser window. Take some time to write encouraging feedback in the comment box.
Then click one of

Comment: just general feedback or you’re being nosey.
Approve: this PR is worthy of main.
Request changes: this needs a little work.

as appropriate and then Submit Review.

Comments on code start a “conversation” which can be resolved. It is up to the reviewer to resolve conversations.
I’d encourage authors to use emoji reactions or responding to comments to track their work.
You can view changes incurred by a particular commit. Clicking the commit ID on the commit history (main page of the PR) will show you these changes. This is really useful in the ping-pong (review back-and-forth) stage of the review to isolate changes, rather looking through the entire PR again.

title: About
text:
I’m Jack, a statistician, data scientist and educator based in the north east. Nice to meet you.
I’m currently a senior data scientist at UKHSA primarily working on short-term forecasting and nowcasting models for seasonal pathogens and outbreak response. I completed all my studies at Newcastle University. I hold a PhD in Statistics (2023) and also obtained a First class MMathStat (2018) and continue to make the occasional academic contributions.
From a professional perspective, I am interested in epidemic modelling, RAP, production-ready modelling software, technical leadership and team structures, and developing others. I’ve donated a lot of my time to the Royal Statistical Society; serving and chairing the Young Statisticians Section, I’m also treasurer or the North Eastern local group and have made many contributions to their annual conference programme.
When I’m not doing massive nerd stuff I’m probably doing some type II fun. I fill my free time with cycling, climbing and walking the dog. The dog is called Robin and I don’t know what breed he is.

title: Unidentified forecasting object
text:
Okay so this isn’t mega serious but this data is real. A few years ago a wrote a Jumping Rivers blog post about using Stan to model global UFO sightings reports. The #TidyTuesday project has used this data set before to prompt some fun visualisations. I used splines in time and a negative binomial distribution to model a reporting pattern.
A few years have passed since then and I’ve been working in epidemiology for a while. A common statistical approach to short term forecasting (forecasts of up to about 4 weeks ahead) for epidemics is to use splines in time and a negative binomial distribution to describe key quantities of interest. For example, the number of cases of a novel pathogen reported daily by some geographical region (e.g. different countries, or in the US we might model disease dynamics at state level).
I’ve gotten used to working with that kind of data and I’ve been itching to revisit that blog post with 3ish years worth of epidemic modelling under my belt. The analysis I’ll be doing here will be based upon open source code from the modelling I do in my day job.
The plan here is to build a mini epidemiological-style modelling pipeline to predict the number of UFO sighting reports at various locations. We will need need a little primer on ensemble modelling and GAMs, but before we do that, let’s have a look at the data.

title: Unidentified forecasting object
text:
Ensembles
Ensemble methods essentially take the predictions from multiple statistical models and combine them in the hope you achieve an overall more accurate forecast. Ensembles tend to be more robust than single-model predictions in two senses:

Statistically robust: different models encode different assumptions. By ensembling, we are not relying on a single set of assumptions for our analysis.
Operationally robust: code breaks, models sometimes behave weird, data feeds vanish with no prior warning. If we can’t get a model to run, or the output is not an epidemiologically plausible prediction, we can drop a models contribution to an ensemble and still output a forecast.

So when you’re fitting models every week to deliver to important people (politicians, scientists with Wikipedia pages, people who work to save lives), you really can’t afford to put all your eggs in one basket.
It is well known in the epidemiological forecasting literature that a diverse set of models tends to lead to a better ensemble. That means ensembling different assumptions as well as methods. Ensembles can include statistical models (e.g. GAMs - more on those later), mechanistic models like the SIR model, and classic time series model (e.g. ARMA). There’s plenty of other things you can throw in too!

Quantile averaging
There are two ways that are commonly used in my field to construct ensembles. In quantile averaging we take a set of quantiles from a set of models, then the quantiles of the ensemble are the average values of the quantiles from each contributing model. If \(q^m(p)\) is the \(p\%\) quantile of the prediction from model \(m\), then we can map the following component model quantiles to ensemble quantiles:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} q^1(0.05) \\ q^1(0.10) \\ \vdots  \\ q^1(0.50) \\\vdots \\ q^1(0.90) \\ q^1(0.95) \end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix} q^2(0.05) \\ q^2(0.10) \\ \vdots  \\ q^2(0.50) \\ \vdots \\q^2(0.90) \\ q^2(0.95) \end{pmatrix},
\ldots,
\begin{pmatrix} q^M(0.05) \\ q^M(0.10) \\ \vdots  \\ q^M(0.50) \\ \vdots \\ q^M(0.90) \\ q^M(0.95) \end{pmatrix}
\overset{\text{ensemble}}{\rightarrow}
\begin{pmatrix} \bar{q}(0.05) \\ \bar{q}(0.10) \\ \vdots  \\ \bar{q}(0.50) \\ \vdots \\\bar{q}(0.90) \\ \bar{q}(0.95) \end{pmatrix}
\] Here we’ve used the mean to average the quantiles. The median of the quantiles might also be used.
The method is great for “forecasting hubs”. Lots of public health agencies allow modelling teams to submit there own forecasts of a epidemic as a collection of quantiles, then the hub aggregates the submitted predictions and outputs ensemble. For example, the US’s CDC had a COVID-19 forecasting hub. It’s an efficient way to construct ensembles, however, the mean of a collection of quantiles is not the same as the “true” quantile of the ensemble.


Posterior stacking
Suppose I can generate predictive samples from my model. For most statistical models, this is quite simple as we’ve assumed some statistical form and then fit a model to the data. If we then generate \(N\) samples from each the \(M\) ensemble models, we then have \(N \times M\) samples, from which we can compute quantiles.
The nice thing about posterior stacking is it gives us a coherent forecast when we have breakdowns in our predictions. It’s not uncommon for the spread of a disease through a population to somehow depends on the characteristics of sub-populations. For example, very young or very old people tend to have weaker immune systems so are more likely to have severe symptoms of a disease. Some countries or regions within a country take different approaches to public heath (for reasons which might be political choices or driven by the availability of resources) and therefore we expect an epidemic to be worse in some locations compared to others.
We might want forecasts of individual regions within a country, but then also want a national forecast. To obtain a national forecast we just sum the regional forecasts. If we used a quantile-averaging approach the quantiles of the sums might not equal the sums of the quantiles, but if we sum samples and then compute quantiles, we obtain a coherent forecast. The downside of this approach is submitting lots of samples to a hub can get a bit messy, so the stacking method is often preferred by those producing ensembles “in house”.

title: Unidentified forecasting object
text:
Building up an ensemble
Now we’ve built a single-model forecast, we want to scale up to an ensemble-based workflow. I’m going to use the {purrr} package and a neat little trick to generate our ensemble with (excluding the model functions themselves), just two function calls!
If you’re not familiar with {purrr}, purrr:map() lets us iterate over elements of a list, it’s basically an implementation of a for loop or reframing of apply() type functions. Remember earlier I stored all my model functions in a named list called models? Well I can purrr::map() over these models and stack all the results in a data frame to create our ensemble. I’d used purrr::map() a lot in the past to iterate over data (e.g. apply the same functions to different data sets), but the first time I saw the inverse: apply different functions to the same data I thought that was actually pretty cool.

model_fits <- models |>
  # fit each element of models to the data (and generate a forecast)
  purrr::map(\(.m) .m(fit_data, forecast_horizon)) |>
  # stack the predictions up in to a single data frame
  dplyr::bind_rows()

And that’s it, model_fits is literally our ensemble. We can then compute summaries of this set of samples to visualise and communicate our forecasts. You can expand the below code, but the idea is basically the same as for a single model since we’ve used posterior stacking to construct our ensemble.


Show code
ensemble_summary <- model_fits |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    
    pi_05 = quantile(.response, 0.05),
    pi_25 = quantile(.response, 0.25),
    pi_50 = quantile(.response, 0.50),
    pi_75 = quantile(.response, 0.75),
    pi_95 = quantile(.response, 0.95),
    
    .by = c(month_year, country_code, type)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(model_ready, month_year, country_code, sightings_month),
    by = c("month_year", "country_code")
  )

ensemble_summary |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_05, ymax = pi_95, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_25, ymax = pi_75, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = pi_50, colour = type)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = sightings_month), size = 0.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = fit_data,
    mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = sightings_month), size = 0.1) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(ggplot2::vars(country_code), scale = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Report date",
    y = "Monthly UFO sighting reports"
  ) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle(
    "National predictions with observed number of reports",
    subtitle = "Median prediction with 50% and 90% predictive intervals"
  )









And that’s our set of national UFO sighting report forecasts – to be honest in this case they’re not too dissimilar to the Gaussian process forecast. The ensemble seems to be a bit smoother, and we’re still overshooting the true number of reports in GB. It’s likely we could improve this forecast significantly with model tuning, but that’s beyond the scope of what I want to do here.
Finally, we can produce a “Global” forecast based off the subset of countries we’ve constructed our ensemble on. It’s not a true global forecast as we have only modelled a small number of countries. Since we’re using posterior stacking, our global forecast is literally just the sum of the national forecasts, just remember to compute quantiles after aggregating for coherence.

# add up predictions across each country
ensemble_summary_global <- model_fits |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    .response = sum(.response),
    .by = c(month_year, name, .draw, type)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    
    pi_05 = quantile(.response, 0.05),
    pi_25 = quantile(.response, 0.25),
    pi_50 = quantile(.response, 0.50),
    pi_75 = quantile(.response, 0.75),
    pi_95 = quantile(.response, 0.95),
    
    .by = c(month_year, type)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    # we need national sums of true data too
    model_ready |>
      dplyr::summarise(sightings_month = sum(sightings_month), .by = month_year),
    by = c("month_year")
  )

Our global ensemble forecast is pretty good! In my own experience, aggregate forecasts are usually more reliable than the lower-level forecasts as the overall curve is a bit smoother, and the weird local variations get diluted in the bigger picture.

fit_data_global <- fit_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(sightings_month = sum(sightings_month), .by = month_year)

ensemble_summary_global |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_05, ymax = pi_95, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_25, ymax = pi_75, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = pi_50, colour = type)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = sightings_month), size = 0.1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Report date",
    y = "Monthly UFO sighting reports"
  ) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle(
    "Aggregate prediction with observed number of reports",
    subtitle = "Median prediction with 50% and 90% predictive intervals"
  )

title: Unidentified forecasting object
section: A forecast of future UFO sighting reports
text:
A forecast of future UFO sighting reports
It’s great that we’ve produced something that can produce a reasonable retrospective forecast of UFO sighting reports, but what can we expect to happen into the future? This data only goes up to 2023, so let’s make a 10-year ahead forecast to bring us up to 2033. This is a much longer forecast horizon than we would usually make with this kind of model! All we do here is modify our forecast horizon and then make sure we using all available data (rather than chopping time off to do a retrospective fit). I’ll just do this at the global level, but the logic transfers to national-level forecast in a similar way.


Show code
forecast_horizon <- 12 * 10

forecast <- models |>
  # fit each element of models to the data (and generate a forecast)
  purrr::map(\(.m) .m(model_ready, forecast_horizon)) |>
  # stack the predictions up in to a single data frame
  dplyr::bind_rows()
  
ensemble_forecast_global <- forecast |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    .response = sum(.response),
    .by = c(month_year, name, .draw, type)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    
    pi_05 = quantile(.response, 0.05),
    pi_25 = quantile(.response, 0.25),
    pi_50 = quantile(.response, 0.50),
    pi_75 = quantile(.response, 0.75),
    pi_95 = quantile(.response, 0.95),
    
    .by = c(month_year, type)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    # we need national sums of true data too
    model_ready |>
      dplyr::summarise(sightings_month = sum(sightings_month), .by = month_year),
    by = "month_year"
  )

ensemble_forecast_global |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_05, ymax = pi_95, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, ymin = pi_25, ymax = pi_75, fill = type),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = pi_50, colour = type)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(x = month_year, y = sightings_month), size = 0.1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = plot_colours) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Report date",
    y = "Monthly UFO sighting reports"
  ) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle(
    "10 year ahead prediction for monthly UFO sighting reports",
    subtitle = "Median prediction with 50% and 90% predictive intervals"
  )









Up to about 2030 the forecast looks reasonable, we see a gradually decreasing trend towards very few monthly sighting reports. After 2030, then the model uncertainty just explodes to the point where the uncertainty is so wide that the prediction is probably not that useful for people making decisions based off, ahem, the number of UFO sighting reports made every month.
